newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl says Germany not sure how to plug budget hole.
newsitem.headline: Kohl says Germany not sure how to plug budget hole.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl admitted on Friday the government did not yet know how it would fill new holes in its budget.
But in a rousing, impromptu speech in parliament, Kohl lashed out at the opposition Social Democrats, saying they had blocked his efforts to cut unemployment and taxes.
"You want to drive the country into the ground in order to win the next election," said Kohl, red faced with anger as he spoke to a hastily called lower house debate on a new budget shortfall.

"The long overdue tax reform would have got much further if you had been willing to talk with us," Kohl said, turning towards the SPD benches. "For years you have been fighting against (reform) in an unbelievable and demogogic fashion."
Responding to demands from the SPD that the government inform parliament how it will plug the budget gap, Kohl said the coalition needed some time to work out a plan.
"It has to be carefully considered," Kohl said.

"We need a moment to contemplate. In July we will set out a new budget outline. At that point it will be decided whether we need a supplementary budget. But you can't expect us to give you answers today that we don't have."

Saying he was confident the economy would continue growing steadily at 2.5 percent this year and unemployment would begin to fall towards the end of the year, Kohl told deputies Germany urgently needed to push through a sweeping tax reform.
"We need investment in order to reduce unemployment," Kohl said.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel officially informed parliament that tax revenues for 1997 would be 18 billion marks ($10.6 billion) less than expected.
Along with the huge cost of unexpectedly high unemployment already burdening the budget, the tax shortfall will make it hard for Germany to qualify for the single European currency.
Waigel urged the SPD, which controls the upper house of parliament, to return to talks with the government on a sweeping tax reform programme. The talks collapsed last month.
He told deputies tax revenues were down because of low inflation, increased efforts by Germans to avoid tax, and schemes by firms to shift a greater portion of profits abroad.
"The numbers we have seen in the last few days are a clear indication that we need to push through reform," Kohl said.
"The major tax reform is completely overdue now and it absolutely has to be implemented."

Praising reforms carried out by the government in the Netherlands, Kohl made an offer to SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping to invite Prime Minister Wim Kok of the left-leaning Labour Party to Germany to act as arbitrator.
On Thursday Waigel had said he wanted to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves and accelerate the pace of privatisation to fill the budget gaps. Tax increases were also a possibility, he said.
SPD parliamentary group leader Rudolf Scharping said it was astonishing that the government was blaming everyone but itself.

"The hole is so big now that the whole coalition could fit in there," Scharping said. "You have irresponsibly clouded the issues. You have no concept. You blame everyone else. You have lousy excuses for everything."

He accused Waigel of damaging Germany's reputation with the Bundesbank gold plan. "You have harmed Germany's standing and are now going about harming our standing in international markets," he said. "It is irresponsible."
